# Penicillin (antibiotics from mould) (`penicillin`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/medicine.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`)
- Deps: needs microorganisms, heat_sterilisation, contagion_theory; helped by microscope, refrigeration, acids_bases_ph, controlled_trial
- Core idea: Certain Penicillium moulds produce a substance that blocks cell-wall construction in susceptible, growing bacteria. A clear zone around a mould colony demonstrates inhibition; it does not establish purity, dose or safety in a patient. The Oxford team had to recover an unstable substance, measure its activity and obtain enough sterile drug for sustained treatment. Different penicillins differ in their stability in stomach acid. Benefit depends on the infecting organism and its susceptibility. Serious allergy is possible, and mould or crude filtrate cannot substitute for a tested medicine.
- Pitfalls:
  - Putting mouldy bread on a wound or eating it; too little penicillin, the wrong moulds, and some moulds make poisons
  - Assuming any green mould will do, or that Fleming's 1928 observation was already a medicine; it took a team twelve more years
  - Expecting it to cure plague, tuberculosis, typhoid, cholera, malaria or virus diseases such as smallpox and influenza
  - Running out mid-treatment: an early Oxford patient, Albert Alexander, improved and then died in 1941 when the supply ended
  - Forgetting allergy, which can kill within minutes, and that under-dosing breeds resistant germs
- History: europe: 1870s – Burdon-Sanderson, Lister and Tyndall note that moulds suppress bacteria; 1897 Duchesne's thesis in Lyon; 1928 Fleming (published 1929); 1930 Cecil Paine documents topical treatment of eye infections in Sheffield; 1939–1941 Florey, Chain, Heatley and colleagues develop systemic treatment in Oxford; americas: 1941–1944 – Peoria laboratory and US firms develop deep-tank fermentation, corn-steep liquor and a high-yield strain from a mouldy cantaloupe; enough for the Allied armies by June 1944
- Read:
  - Alexander Fleming, On the antibacterial action of cultures of a Penicillium, with special reference to their use in the isolation of B. influenzae, British Journal of Experimental Pathology (1929)
  - Eric Lax, The Mould in Dr Florey's Coat (2004)
  - Robert Bud, Penicillin: Triumph and Tragedy (2007)
  - M. Wainwright and H. T. Swan, C. G. Paine and the earliest surviving clinical records of penicillin therapy, Medical History (1986)
